summary: Observation of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On December 31, 2010, at approximately 11:30 PM, a witness observed the movement of an intense red spot. The witness heard no unusual noise as the spot approached, then abruptly changed direction and rapidly moved away on an upward trajectory. After viewing the video and photos on the GEIPAN website, the witness confirmed that he had seen a Thai lantern.

summary: Long observation of the evolution of rings and bright points in the sky: lack of information.
description: On December 30, 2010, at 6:30 PM, a witness observed, in a partly cloudy sky, the movement of several white ovoid rings and luminous points. The observation lasted 45 minutes. The description of the UAP, consisting of a multitude of white luminous streaks with periodic movements, suggests the observation of a light show from a Skyrose-type multi-beam projector. These projectors are frequently a source of confusion due to the unusual patterns they project onto clouds, and whose beams are not necessarily visible when the atmosphere is clear, such as after rain. However, in this case, the witness reported a dark sky, with few stars but also only a few clouds (see QT p. 5/8). While the sky should have been clear given the strong winds throughout the day, the detailed weather data in section 3.1 indicates fog and drizzle in Le Havre, Dieppe, and Rouen, and the incomplete satellite images do not allow us to know the cloud cover at the time of observation. Based on this (fog), the atmospheric conditions do not seem compatible with observing lights projected onto the cloud cover, as the fog should have revealed the beams and therefore the direction of the spotlight. Furthermore, there no longer appears to be a nightclub in Senneville, but the announcement of an exceptional New Year's Eve party may have motivated a party organizer. Of low strangeness and average consistency, this observation cannot be definitively concluded, although the hypothesis of a Skyrose-type projector, entirely consistent with the observation report, seems plausible on New Year's Eve. This case is classified as Class C due to a lack of independent witness statements and corroborating evidence.

summary: Repeated sightings of a black mass with yellow lights and a red flashing light; a deep, muffled engine noise: probable sighting of a helicopter.
description: On December 27, 2010, at 6:45 PM, a motorist was intrigued by a phenomenon on the left side of the D937 road near the hamlet of La Boule d'Or in Geneston (44). He saw a dark mass with two yellow lights underneath it. The witness described these lights as rotating, revealing about ten other yellow lights. The observation lasted between 5 and 6 seconds. The motorist pulled over to the side of the road but did not see the phenomenon again. Continuing on his way, he saw the UFO again, passing overhead, but the darkness and mist prevented him from clearly distinguishing the object's outline. The UFO made a rather muffled, deep engine noise; a beam at the front and a red flashing light were visible. The motorist saw the UFO one last time, high in the air a little further along the road. Only one witness statement was recorded. There is every reason to believe that the witness saw an aircraft (and probably a helicopter). The witness himself makes this hypothesis towards the end of his observation: "I remember thinking this time it was a plane because Nantes airport is in that direction." Above all, the witness does not introduce any strangeness that he would explicitly oppose to this aircraft hypothesis and the descriptive elements ("succession of yellow lights like portholes", "oval shape", "engine noise, quite muffled and deep like that of a wind tunnel", "headlight whose beam was mobile, agitated by very rapid oblique movements but without a great range, because it only illuminated the clouds a few meters in front of the aircraft", "very powerful red gyro beacon and on the other side an identical gyro beacon but in blue colors, the same shade as that of the rescue vehicles") are compatible with an aircraft, and more probably with a helicopter given the particular lighting of the latter (including rotating spotlights), the proximity of hospitals and the rather slow movement. The witness mentions the presence of heavy road traffic and the lack of reaction, which supports the claim that it was perceived as an aircraft without any notable unusual features. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable helicopter sighting.

summary: Probable observation of an aircraft passing overhead.
description: On December 5, 2010, at approximately 11:45 PM, a driver and his passenger observed an unexplained object in the sky. A cylindrical object, luminous at the front and rear, crossed the sky. As indicated by the witness himself in the questionnaire, this observation corresponds to the probable sighting of the two approach lights of an aircraft through the hazy and polluted skies of the Paris metropolitan area. The questionnaire is not very detailed and does not allow for a more in-depth interpretation.

summary: Observation of several bright points in the sky originating from pyrotechnic lances attached to Thai lanterns.
description: On Friday, December 3, 2010, at 7:17 p.m., a driver and his passenger noticed a group of white lights with a purplish sheen in the sky. The phenomenon gradually disappeared. The first-level responder, tasked with further investigation, obtained confirmation from the Riedisheim town hall that a humanitarian organization had organized a release of "light balloons" that evening. Pyrotechnic "concrete" (of the Blinklanzen type from Switzerland) had been attached to helium-filled balloons. No photographs were taken, but the confirmation from the town hall and the information provided leave no doubt as to the event. The case is therefore clearly identified.

summary: Observations of rapid movements of 5 to 6 yellow-orange luminous points and a fixed luminous point: lack of information.
description: On November 26, 2010, between 11:30 p.m. and midnight, two witnesses observed five or six luminous points of the same size and a yellow-orange color in the sky. These points moved silently in rapid, erratic curves around another, fixed point of light. The points went out abruptly, while the witnesses noticed that the fixed point gradually faded. GEIPAN considered several hypotheses for this observation: initially, Thai lanterns, but one of the witnesses stated that the movements of the lights were far too rapid and centered on a fixed point. A pyrotechnic or electrical display set up for a celebration was also considered, but there did not appear to have been any major celebration in Mirande that day. A "natural" cause was ruled out, given the complexity of the observed movements. As the events are too far in the past to seek other witnesses and launch an investigation, this case is classified as category "C" due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation of three colored lights passing through, outlining a dark triangular shape. A rustling sound of air was heard: unexplained phenomenon.
description: On November 21, 2010, at 5:55 PM, a person opening their kitchen window on the 9th floor of their apartment was intrigued by the unusual presence of a luminous phenomenon to the east. In the cloudy sky, the witness observed three lights (one red and two blue) arranged in a triangle, rapidly approaching their building. The witness then saw a darker, triangular shape defined by these lights and heard a rustling sound in the air. The phenomenon disappeared as it passed over the building. The observation lasted between 10 and 15 seconds. No other accounts were collected. This testimony is considered quite substantial thanks to a very thorough questionnaire and a field investigation that confirmed the elements of the observation. Nevertheless, it remains a unique account with all the uncertainties that entails. This observation is highly unusual: the phenomenon does not resemble the most well-known misinterpretations. It should be noted, however, that although it resembles no known flying object, the movement of the phenomenon remains within the dynamic range of current flying objects. Due to its good consistency and high degree of strangeness, this case is classified as D1, meaning unexplained.

summary: Unknown objects in photographs without direct observation during the shooting: probably reflections on the vehicle window.
description: On November 17, 2010, at 9:38 a.m., a motorist took photographs with his cell phone through the window of his moving vehicle and noticed, three months later, unfamiliar luminous objects in the photographs. At the time the photos were taken, the sky was clear with intense morning sunlight (see one of the witness photos). In the absence of a police report and a detailed witness statement, these photos most likely show reflections on the vehicle's window of one or more objects located inside the vehicle. The police report arrived at GEIPAN on March 8, 2011. The witness confirmed his earlier observations. The police investigation was unable to uncover any further witness statements.

summary: Observation in the sky at a significant distance of a saucer-shaped luminous phenomenon: lack of information.
description: On November 16, 2010, at 6:40 a.m., a motorist observed a fixed, luminous, saucer-shaped object in the sky for two to three minutes at a considerable distance (several kilometers). The object's perimeter was adorned with about thirty white and green lights. He got out of his vehicle to take a picture with his cell phone, but the sensitivity was insufficient. He put his phone away and, looking back towards the UFO, found it had disappeared. No other witness accounts were collected. The strangeness of this sighting depends primarily on the witness's interpretation of the observed phenomenon: if one takes into account the saucer-shaped description of the UFO, the strangeness becomes very significant. If we consider that the object was too distant for this interpretation to be relevant, the strangeness of the case becomes less pronounced and leaves open the possibility of a simple confusion with a star (this confusion is frequent for stars or planets observed low on the horizon). Furthermore, this case is of average to weak consistency due to the imprecision of the position and direction of observation, and the absence of a photograph. GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to a lack of corroborating evidence.

summary: Observation of a black dot moving in the sky: observation of a festive helium balloon.
description: On November 14, 2011, between 3:50 and 4:00 PM, a witness filmed the movement of a black dot in the cloudy sky. By zooming in sharply with their camcorder, a dark object appeared. Viewing the footage strongly suggests the movement of a helium balloon. The observed direction of movement is consistent with a southeast wind. Of low strangeness and moderate consistency, this observation is most likely the result of confusion with a helium-filled party balloon. This case is classified as Class A.

summary: Observations two days apart of the movement of three lights forming a triangle, sudden disappearances: lack of information.
description: On the evening of Tuesday, November 9, 2010, at midnight, the witness, in his apartment kitchen, was observing the stars when he noticed a group of three yellowish lights moving in a triangle. The observation was abruptly interrupted by the disappearance of the three lights and lasted barely two seconds. A few days later, the same observation was repeated (date, time, duration, and circumstances not specified). The satellite hypothesis is not suitable at this time of night. The yellowish color and the movement consistent with the wind direction suggest a case of mistaken identity with Thai lanterns seen at the moment they were extinguished. These lanterns are generally licked during festivities, most often on weekends. The very short duration of the observation does not allow for confirmation of this hypothesis, which nevertheless remains possible. Finally, the witness does not specify whether the observation took place with the window open or closed. We can therefore also consider the possibility of a reflection from a kitchen light fixture where the witness was standing. Due to its weak consistency and the difficulty in assessing its strangeness because of the very short observation period, this case cannot be concluded. This case is classified as C due to a lack of independent witness statements and corroborating evidence.

summary: Probable sighting of the star Sirius.
description: A witness, driving at high speed (130 km/h), observed an intense white halo swirling in the sky. The information provided in the questionnaire (no police report was filed) does not specify the exact location or duration of the observation. However, the vehicle was traveling north to south, and the driver was looking south through the windshield. At the time of the observation, Sirius, the brightest star in our sky, was in the direction of observation. The variable, scintillating nature of the halo, combined with visual fatigue from driving, could explain the swirling appearance of the observation. Precise verification is not possible, but the likely observation of Sirius could explain the event.

summary: Probable observation of a remotely piloted flying object.
description: witness belatedly reported (official report dated April 14, 2011) an observation made between 2:40 PM and 3:10 PM at the beginning of November 2010 (November 2, 8, 9, or 10, 2010). While walking his dog on a country road, a witness was fascinated for about ten seconds by an object he could not identify. Flying approximately 2.5 meters above the ground, a blue object moved at a steady speed along a straight trajectory. The witness described a cubic shape with two white circles on either side connected by beams of light. The object crossed the road in front of the witness and suddenly disappeared near a tree. The witness found no trace of the object in the tree branches. No other witness statements were collected regarding this phenomenon, and no particular traces were found at the scene by the police, who were notified late. The hypothesis considered in the IPN investigation of a remotely piloted flying object or a quadcopter-type drone could correspond to the description. These devices are proliferating, are sold everywhere, at all prices, in all sizes and colors (some can be controlled by an iPhone). The characteristics of 'blurriness' around the body ('cube with rounded corners') described by the witness could correspond to the rotation of the associated wings, the witness's visual acuity not allowing them to distinguish the details of an object, nor to accurately judge distances. This observation presents a low degree of strangeness, without a precise date of observation. The majority of the characteristics described correspond to those of known objects (remote-controlled object, drone, etc.). This case is classified as Class B, like the probable observation of a remotely piloted object (toy, drone).

summary: Observation of a particularly bright point and the presence of points of several colors in the sky: probable astronomical observation of Jupiter.
description: Recent report (October 11, 2012) of a past observation. A witness observed a bright object in the sky through binoculars at 1:20 AM on October 9, 2010. The witness was astonished by the brightness and the observation of colored points of light. The star chart, oriented according to the witness's direction of observation (South-Southwest), showed the presence of the planet Jupiter, with a magnitude of -2.9, that is, brighter than all the stars in the sky. From 1:20 AM to 2:20 AM, it moved westward from an azimuth of 193° to 220°, and its elevation dropped from 40° to 36°. The witness indicated the object to the Southwest (South + 45° West: 225°), very bright, especially compared to the stars, which were barely visible. A fairly humid southeast wind was observed, clearing the sky, obscuring the fainter stars, and causing strong twinkling: this likely explains the green/white/red color changes observed by the witness. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B," a probable observation of Jupiter. The discrepancies of approximately 20 arcseconds between the observer's readings and the astronomical position leave an uncertainty that prevents classifying this case as "A."

summary: Observation of the passage of a dark triangular phenomenon with flashing white lights at the extremities and a flashing red light in the center: lack of information.
description: On October 6, 2010, at 8:17 PM, two people observed a phenomenon flying over the Golfech nuclear power plant from outside a building. It was described as a black triangle with flashing white lights at the extremities and a flashing red light in the center. The object flew at low altitude in a dark, cloudy sky. No noise was heard. One of the witnesses (T2) recorded a video on his cell phone before the object gradually disappeared in the direction of Saint-Loup. An initial investigation led GEIPAN (the French group investigating and investigating nuclear phenomena) to conclude on November 22, 2012, that it was likely an aircraft sighting. A further investigation was conducted in October 2013 due to the possibility of accessing the Golfech power plant site. Several hypotheses (EDF maintenance equipment, airplane, drone, hoax, UAP D) will be considered (see the investigation report). This complex observation case presented GEIPAN with a methodological problem due to the following elements, which significantly weaken the case: - The two witnesses interpret the phenomenon very differently. - T2's statements to the police are unfavorable to the witness. - The video, considered evidence by T1, turns out to be a video of streetlights. Aside from the fact that it is obviously not evidence, this video could have influenced the testimony after the fact, if the witness unconsciously aligned their account with the video at the expense of remembering their own vision of the phenomenon. - T2 appears easily influenced, as evidenced by his statement to the police and the interview he gave to C. Albiero. Under these circumstances, it is unclear what weight to give to his statements, while also not being able to ignore his testimony. Therefore, GEIPAN assigned a value of 0.6 to the consistency of this case, a lower value than that assigned to a typical single witness (0.7). Furthermore, the aircraft hypothesis, initially proposed by GEIPAN, suffers from several inconsistencies (see the investigation report); it would only be acceptable if one were to consider both significant distortions in the testimonies and the existence of a low-altitude aircraft undetected by radar or the control center's surveillance. GEIPAN considers as certain the passage of three flashing lights arranged in a triangle around a flashing red light. The black triangle mentioned by witnesses is probably the result of the common illusion known as the "black triangle" or "black triangle" illusion: the actual object could be either a set of four independent light sources or a craft much larger than the triangle described by the witnesses (the airplane hypothesis or something else). The altitude is undeterminable, as in all cases of nighttime observations of luminous points: the witnesses here estimate very different altitudes, which is quite normal; it is very likely that the true altitude of the luminous phenomenon is different again. The strangeness of the phenomenon was judged to be moderate to high (0.55) since the closest hypothesis (airplane) suffers from several elements inconsistent with the observation. We are faced with a case of average consistency and strangeness, bordering on categories B, C, and D: a slight difference in the assessment of strangeness or consistency would allow it to be classified in the neighboring categories. Due to this sensitivity, GEIPAN sought the opinion of its expert panel, which met on April 12, 2016, in Paris. The opinions were divided as follows: 4 experts voted for classification in D1, considering the luminous phenomenon that passed over the nuclear power plant to be unexplained. 8 experts voted for classification in C, considering the evidence in the file contained too many inconsistencies to provide a definitive opinion. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies this case in category C due to insufficiently reliable information.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On September 25, 2010, at approximately 11:30 PM, a witness observed eight orange orbs silently passing by from their garden. The characteristics of the observation (several orange orbs flying silently in the same direction, seen in successive bursts and then disappearing, observed over a period of 15-20 minutes), as well as the date and time (Saturday night/Sunday morning around midnight) and the reconstruction/drawings made by the main witness, correspond to a known phenomenon of flying lanterns. The NW:310E wind corresponds to the direction of movement described by the witness ("coming from the West and heading towards the East"). The level of strangeness of the observation is low, and the probable hypothesis of a flight of Thai-type lanterns is highly likely. The case is classified as Class B.

summary: Observation of a tethered balloon in the shape of a dirigible.
description: On September 24, 2010, motorists traveling on the A11 motorway (Le Mans-Paris direction) noticed a stationary object in the sky that intrigued them. The witnesses, having reached the Sarge-les-Le-Mans rest area, photographed a dark gray, airship-like structure with no mooring points, which appeared motionless throughout the observation. Continuing their journey, they lost sight of the object. A statement from another witness indicated that it was a tethered balloon (connected by a long cable), hovering above the Auvours military camp, located in Champagne (72).

summary: Probable observation of balloon flight.
description: On September 19, 2010, several people observed five to seven bright white dots around 4:30 PM, which intrigued them. No trails or noises were noticed during the objects' slow northeastward movement. Photographs were taken during the forty-minute observation. Only one person provided a statement and sent us the original photographs with commentary. The characteristics of the observation (two, then several white dots drifting rather slowly "as if carried by the wind") as well as photos P1070304 and P1070306 most likely indicate a flight of balloons. The witness himself mentioned the possibility of "weather balloons." The date of the observation (Sunday afternoon) could correspond to a flight of small festive balloons. This case presents a low level of strangeness. It is most likely explained by a flight of balloons.

summary: Observation of the silent movement OE of a black and round object in the sky: probable observation of a festive balloon.
description: On September 19, 2010, at 7:45 PM, a witness observed from their home the presence and silent movement of a round, black flying object. The witness took photographs of the object. No other witness statements were collected. The photographs strongly suggest a festive helium balloon adorned with ribbons, or one of a somewhat complex shape. Although made from reflective materials such as Mylar, the dark color is explained by the fact that the photographs were taken against the light, facing west-southwest at sunset. The object's slow, straight movement is consistent with the prevailing wind and most likely originated from the numerous sales points scattered around Parisian tourist sites. Of low strangeness and medium consistency, this observation most likely resulted from a case of mistaken identity involving a helium party balloon that escaped its owner's control. This case is class B.

summary: Observation of the movement of advertising balloons in the sky.
description: On September 11, 2010, at 5:30 PM, several people observed the slow movement of about ten bright white dots in the sky. No noise was heard during the 10-minute observation. The photograph taken by the witness immediately led to the possibility of a balloon launch. An internet search revealed that a fashion show had taken place to the south-southwest of the observation site (information repeated in a local press article). This show concluded with a balloon release (information confirmed by the organizer contacted by GEIPAN) around 5:30 PM. The weather conditions, with a light south-southwest wind, caused these balloons to fly over the beach at the observation site. This case is classified as Class A, indicating a balloon sighting.

summary: Observing Jupiter.
description: On September 10, 2010, at approximately 10:30 PM, a witness observed a very bright object moving at a very high altitude in the sky for 40 minutes. The characteristics of the observation (a very bright object in the night sky, and the 40-minute observation period, which was interrupted by the witness while the phenomenon was still visible) suggest the observation of a celestial object. The configuration of the sky indicated the presence of the planet Jupiter, with a magnitude of -2.9 (visible to the naked eye), in the southeast sector of the observation site. The event is classified as Class A, like the observation of the planet Jupiter.

summary: Observations of the movement of luminous phenomena in the sky: probable observation of the passage of the International Space Station (ISS).
description: On September 10, 2010, at 8:49 PM, a witness at home was intrigued by the silent movement of a luminous phenomenon in the sky. Of moderate strangeness due to the possible succession of misinterpretations from different sources, and of good consistency thanks to precise geographical markers on the sketch in 4.1, this observation can be explained, in its first part, by a misinterpretation of the International Space Station (ISS), hence the partial classification suggested in A. For the second part of the observation, it is necessary to introduce new hypotheses, namely a possible aircraft with its approach lights on, or a perceptual illusion (perception of two straight line segments instead of an arc). These hypotheses, which cannot be confirmed, will remain weak. This case is consistent (an eyewitness with a high-quality testimony), and its strangeness is low, since it is fairly well explained by known phenomena. Given the uncertainty on the second part of the observation, this case is class B to: probable observation of the International Space Station (ISS).

summary: Probable observation of the evolution of a Thai lantern.
description: On September 10, 2010, at around 9 p.m., a motorist was intrigued by a luminous orange-red ball that moved slowly, changed color, and then suddenly disappeared. The characteristics of the observation (the white-yellow light of a very large star turning orange-yellow, the ovoid shape appearing stationary, the disappearance (extinction), and the trajectory consistent with the wind direction) suggest a luminous balloon of the Thai lantern type.

summary: Successive observations of the movement of luminous phenomena in the sky: astronomical misinterpretations.
description: witness makes successive observations of a luminous phenomenon moving across the sky. He films his observations. The video footage as a whole corresponds to a case of mistaken identity with the planet Venus. The slow movement perceived relative to the trees is due to the high magnification used (the zoom was probably at its maximum), which reveals the Earth's rotation, imperceptible to the naked eye. Of low oddity and good consistency thanks to the multiple video clips, this case of observation corresponds to multiple misidentifications of the planet Venus for the daytime shots at sunset, and of the planet Jupiter or the ISS for the nighttime shots. This case is class A.

summary: Probable sightings of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: A family reported observing three luminous spheres passing silently by on September 5, 2010, between 1:10 and 1:30 a.m. One of the witnesses took photographs with a cell phone. The characteristics of the sighting (Saturday/Sunday night after midnight, non-dazzling yellow-orange light followed by other lights of the same type, no noise, trajectory at a constant speed consistent with the wind direction) suggest the release of Thai lanterns. The village hall was rented for the same period (wedding, party?). As attempts to contact the village hall for further information received no response, the case is classified as category B, indicating the probable sighting of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the movement of lights.
description: On September 2, 2010, between 3:30 and 4:00 AM, a witness observed several identical yellow lights in the sky, aligned and moving along a north-south trajectory. No sound was heard. The witness did not respond to repeated requests from GEIPAN for further information. Without a police report and due to a lack of information, the case is classified as Class C.

summary: Observation of the fleeting passage of a red object in the sky.
description: A witness in his garden observed a dark red object passing very quickly overhead at 9:58 PM on September 1, 2010. The object's north-south movement was observed for three seconds. No sound was heard. The level of strangeness of the observation is low. The consistency of the observation is also weak (a single witness waiting "to try to observe this type of phenomenon," a very brief observation of a very fleeting phenomenon whose shape the witness struggled to describe). As this testimony is not corroborated by a police report (requested by GEIPAN), any investigation is impossible due to a lack of information. This case is classified as Class C.

summary: Observation of the blinking of a red light moving across the sky: lack of information.
description: On August 31, 2010, at approximately 11:10 PM, a witness observed a flashing red light moving at a constant speed along a linear trajectory in the sky. The particularly long and gradual flashing intrigued the witness. While the sighting was of low oddity and fairly consistent due to the precision of the testimony, this case cannot be concluded due to a lack of further information. The hypothesis of an aircraft equipped with special lighting could be plausible, but could not be confirmed (see the investigation report). This case is classified as Class C due to the lack of independent and corroborating witness statements.

summary: Observation of the movement of a white ball: astronomical observation of Venus.
description: On Tuesday, August 31, 2010, around 9 p.m., a witness, seated at the dinner table, noticed a very bright point of light through the open window of his dining room. Intrigued by what he called "a little sun," he filmed his observation. He made other similar observations. While of low oddity, the evidence from the videos provides good consistency, allowing us to unambiguously classify this case as an A-level case, indicating a misidentification of the planet Venus.

summary: Observation of the movement of about thirty "shuttles" in the sky: observation of Thai lanterns licked on the occasion of a wedding.
description: witness reported an observation made on Sunday, August 29, 2010, around 12:20 a.m. From the first floor of his home, he observed about thirty "shuttles" flying below the cloud cover. All moved slowly from the horizon and passed through the zenith before disappearing, hidden by the urban landscape. A video was recorded with a mobile phone. Unfortunately, the video is very poor, as it doesn't accurately reflect the witness's observation. No particular noise was heard during the observation, except for a slight rumbling in the distance at times. Only one testimony was collected by the gendarmerie (combining report 703 with the questionnaire and report 1073 with additional information from the witness) and by GEIPAN. The video sent by the witness is very similar to the numerous similar videos received by GEIPAN illustrating sightings of Thai lanterns. The characteristics of the observation also correspond: duration, apparent speed, and direction of movement consistent with the local wind. The drawing made by the witness is quite surprising in light of this hypothesis; it is merely a very loose interpretation of a spectacle consisting only of a collection of points of light. A private investigator, contacted directly by the witness, conducted an on-site investigation and concluded: "This is undoubtedly a Thai lantern release during a wedding celebration held in the Tenteling community hall. The bride and groom told me they released 60 lanterns. Everything confirms the reality of this release." GEIPAN classifies this case as "A": observation of Thai lanterns being released during a wedding.

summary: Probable sightings of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On August 29, 2010, at approximately 4:20 a.m., several people observed the slow and silent passage of two orange lights across the sky. The press reported similar sightings later that same day at 9:50 p.m. The description of the phenomenon (reddish-orange spheres moving silently at low altitude) is consistent with those described in cases of Thai lantern sightings. The Sauchay manor frequently hosts wedding ceremonies, and the timing of the observation (Saturday night into Sunday morning) contributes to the high probability of a lantern display.

summary: Observation of the movement of eight orange balls in the sky: probably Thai lanterns.
description: On August 28, 2010, at approximately 10:20 PM, a driver and his passenger observed eight orange orbs moving across the sky in a staggered pattern at an altitude of about 500 meters, following a north-southeast trajectory. The phenomenon lasted approximately four minutes; no noise or odor was perceived. Following receipt of the police report on October 14, 2010, the weather conditions established for the location, date, and time of the observation indicate a north-northwest wind, consistent with the north-southeast movement of lighter-than-air flying objects such as balloons or sky lanterns ("eight orange orbs"). The description of "8 orange balls" moving along "a regular trajectory" together at low altitude (500 meters), during the day (Saturday evening, wedding, party) around 10:30 p.m. local time lends further credence to the observation of a probable passage of Thai lanterns.

summary: Probable sighting of a Thai lantern.
description: On August 26, 2010, two people observed a burning object above their home around 9:20 PM. The object suddenly broke into four separate pieces. Just before igniting, it had a straight trajectory from north to south and was oscillating vertically. No noise was heard during the object's movement or disintegration. The police report and additional administrative information were received by GEIPAN on November 15, 2010. Further investigation revealed that the witness likely observed a Thai lantern from a preliminary test before a large-scale lantern release scheduled for a community festival on the weekend of August 28-29, 2010.

summary: Observing Jupiter.
description: witness observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky at 1:30 a.m. on August 24, 2010, which intrigued him. The described characteristics correspond to those of a known phenomenon (the observation of a planet), and the observation itself presented no unusual features. The presence of the planet Jupiter in the sky at the date and time of the observation, along with characteristic photographs, definitively validates this hypothesis. Although the testimony is unique, it is of good quality, well-detailed, considers different hypotheses, and lends considerable weight to the case. The case is classified as Class A, as explained by the observation of the planet Jupiter.

summary: Observation of the movement of a round, luminous object.
description: On August 22, 2010, at approximately 8:00 PM, a witness observed a round, luminous object for five minutes. The object approached and then disappeared at very high speed to the east. The phenomenon reappeared in the exact same location one minute later and then disappeared very rapidly in a northwest direction. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. The incomplete questionnaire renders this testimony unusable. This case is classified as C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On August 22, 2010, at 2:40 a.m., several people observed from their homes the silent passage of luminous orange orbs forming a triangle and moving in the same south-northeast direction along a straight trajectory. These orbs eventually disappeared after turning a brighter red. One of the witnesses filmed part of the observation. Following a statement given to the police by someone who had read an article about it in the press, and in accordance with the information provided in the police report, this was a confirmed case of lantern licking during a private party in the neighboring town.

summary: Observations of a ballet of luminous balls on a cloudy sky: probable observation of a multi-beam light show.
description: On August 21, 2010, at 11:30 PM, three witnesses observed three balls of light moving rapidly in the cloudy sky from their apartment terrace. The phenomenon disappeared abruptly. Due to its limited strangeness and insufficient detail, lacking any indication of direction or elevation, we cannot definitively identify the origin of what was most likely a multi-beam disco light.

summary: Probable sighting of a flying lantern.
description: The characteristics of the observation (an orange 'fireball' with several peaks inside (fuel flames), stationary or moving slowly, suddenly going out (fuel exhaustion), and the time of observation (Saturday evening around midnight)) strongly suggest the characteristics of a flying lantern sighting. The observation presents a low degree of strangeness. The evidence remains weak (only one witness reported the event through a police report and questionnaire for five witnesses), the other witnesses not having testified directly. The location of the phenomenon is fairly precise and suggests a lecher over the hills opposite the observation site (an existing road). The case is classified as Class B, like the probable sighting of a Thai lantern.

summary: Observations of several luminous objects in the sky: astronomical and astronautical misunderstandings.
description: On Thursday, August 19, 2010, around 2:30 a.m., a witness and their family were intrigued by the presence in the sky of luminous and silent objects (named 1 and 2 in the witness statement), some stationary, others moving. The witness made another observation on August 21, 2010, between 6:00 and 6:30 a.m. (objects named 3 and 4). Objects 1 and 3 are very likely Jupiter, and object 4 is undoubtedly the International Space Station (ISS). Object 2, also stationary and located in the east on August 19, could be the star Capella (azure 47° and 24° elevation, magnitude 0.05). A margin of error in orientation of approximately 45° is commonly observed in witness statements. Of low strangeness and average consistency, this case of observation is the result of several astronomical and astronautical misinterpretations.

summary: Observation of the silent and slow movement of an orange ball: lack of information and cross-checking.
description: On August 19, 2010, at 10:05 PM, a couple observed a very large, slow, and silent movement of an orange sphere across the sky for approximately 30 seconds. Only one witness statement was recorded. This observation of an orange sphere moving horizontally across the sky is reminiscent of a Thai lantern. However, because the witness did not provide the video footage they recorded, nor did they indicate the direction of the movement, GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) was unable to verify this hypothesis. GEIPAN classifies this case as "C" due to a lack of information and corroboration.

summary: Probable sighting of festive balloons passing by.
description: Around 8 p.m., a witness observed a puzzling phenomenon from his fifth-floor balcony for three minutes: above a circular cloud, he saw two groups of objects in the sky, one composed of silvery-white spheres and the other of two red spheres. The north-south movement of these groups was silent. The witness took photographs. The characteristics of the observation suggest a balloon flight. The photos sent to GEIPAN are of poor quality and only allow for the distinction of the two red spheres described by the witness (photo file IMGP0422). It is worth noting that at 9 p.m., the USAP-ASM rugby match took place at the Aimé Guiral stadium in Perpignan, before which balloons could have been released (red is one of the colors of the "blood and gold" team). The observation duration of 3 minutes is consistent with the distance between the stadium and the observation site (approximately 2 km), the wind speed (33 km/h with gusts up to 57 km/h), and the wind direction (NW wind) as reported in the day's weather forecast. The case is classified as Class B, indicating a probable observation of licked balloons approximately 2 km from the observation site.

summary: Regular observations of a luminous and fixed phenomenon in the sky: astronomical observation of Jupiter.
description: The witness observed, for several days in a row, a phenomenon brighter than a star. It appeared in the same location each morning in the southern sky. A textbook example of astronomical misinterpretation, this observation had all the characteristics of a Jupiter sighting, particularly its repeated occurrence from day to day and the brightness typical of nearby planets. This case is Class A, clearly identified as a Jupiter sighting.

summary: Observation of the NS displacement of a luminous phenomenon: lack of information.
description: On August 5, 2010, at 10:55 PM, during a summer walk, a witness observed a bright yellow sphere moving along a north-south trajectory above the city at moderate speed. This somewhat unusual case (a point of light moving in a straight line) is of limited reliability due to inaccuracies in the orientation and description of the phenomenon itself (vague apparent size). The hypothesis of observation of a large satellite remains the most likely, but not proven. This case is classified as Class C due to a lack of information and the noted inaccuracies.

summary: Probable observation of a meteor.
description: On July 30, 2010, at approximately 9:00 PM on the beach at Golfe-Juan, several people observed the rapid and silent passage of an opaque white luminous phenomenon across the sky. Only one eyewitness account was recorded. The characteristics of the object described in this account (a brightly lit ball moving at very high speed for one and a half seconds before disappearing) perfectly match the appearance of a meteor, and in this case, a large shooting star. This case is classified as a Class B probable meteor sighting.

summary: Quick observation of the silent passage of a triangular-shaped object. Presence of a trail: lack of information.
description: On July 30, 2010, at approximately 10:10 PM, a motorist observed a triangular object with two domes on top, passing below the aircraft for a few seconds. The object left a luminous, silvery trail in the sky. No unusual noise was heard during the observation. The object quickly disappeared from the witness's field of vision. No other witness statements were collected. The police report provides no specific information, and the witness did not respond to repeated requests for further information (September 9 by email, November 17 by telephone, and December 16 by telephone, 2010). The case is classified as C due to a lack of information.

summary: Probable sightings of Thai lanterns.
description: On July 28, 2010, at approximately 10:15 PM, several people observed luminous objects resembling hot air balloons. No noise was heard during the five-minute observation. Only one witness reported the sighting. An investigation by the gendarmerie concluded that the objects were likely Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the movement of Thai lanterns.
description: Around 1:30 a.m. on July 25, 2010, two people observed numerous flying objects in the sky from their homes. Triangular or round in shape (according to witnesses) and two-toned, these objects passed over their house in a straight line. No noise was heard during the observations. After checking with the town hall of the witnesses' village, it was discovered that the night of July 24-25 had been marked by festivities in the community, the highlight of which was the release of Thai lanterns at the time specified by the witnesses (as well as by others who contacted the town hall).

summary: Three observations of the presence of a luminous phenomenon in the starry sky: probable mistaking for the beam of a fixed spotlight.
description: On July 20, 2010, between 12:30 a.m. and 5:00 a.m., three people were intrigued by the presence in the starry sky of a luminous phenomenon with a trail that appeared to be moving silently east-west along a straight trajectory. Of moderate strangeness, but with very good consistency (three amateur astronomer witnesses, precise measurements, photograph), this case appears to have been a probable misidentification by the beam of a ground-based spotlight. Numerous possible sources of a fixed spotlight existed near the observation site (buildings, summer commercial activity), and the sky was hazy at altitude. It was not the visual perception of the witnesses that was at fault, but rather their interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (astonishment, initial misinterpretation of the phenomenon, considering it a comet fragmentation, fatigue). This case is classified as Class B, probable misidentification by the beam of a fixed spotlight.

summary: Observation of the movement of about ten circular white and opaque objects in the sky: probable observation of balloons.
description: On July 18, 2010, starting at 5:00 PM, a witness made several successive observations of about ten circular, opaque white objects moving across the sky above Albi. No unusual noise was heard, and no trails or halos were visible. The distance to the phenomenon was estimated to be at least 1500 meters. The observation lasted approximately 40 minutes. Two children also witnessed this phenomenon. The characteristics of the observation resemble those of a known and frequently observed phenomenon involving the movement of festive balloons (daytime observation, the festive period of observation in July, a long observation time of 45 minutes, successive observations of the same phenomena over several periods, opaque white spherical objects, absence of noise, objects moving linearly in the same direction, a northwest-southeast wind direction roughly compatible with the observation, and pinpoint object dimensions). The observation presents no unusual features. The case is weak due to the single witness statement (despite the large number of people who must have been outside at the time). The plausible hypothesis of observing festive balloons (flash balloons) is retained, and this case, with its low level of unusualness, is classified as Class B, as most likely explained.

summary: Probable observation of passing balloons.
description: The questionnaire-based testimony describes the observation of several oblong, dark-colored luminous points (first through binoculars, then with the naked eye). The characteristics of the observation, as well as the date (Sunday morning in July), suggest a formation of sunlit balloons. The direction taken by the first object (to the left of the witness, who was observing towards the south, therefore heading east) and then by the other objects is consistent with the wind direction at the time of the observation. The impression of a "gray trail" described by the witness is surely due to visual persistence. The case is classified as B, as the probable observation of balloons.

summary: Observations of the movement of two oval-shaped objects of metallic grey color: lack of information.
description: On Saturday, July 17, 2010, at approximately 8:45 PM, several members of the same family observed two circular shapes in the southeasterly sky, circling each other. One witness, equipped with binoculars, described two oval shapes of metallic gray with a series of blue lights arranged in a circle below each object. Gaining altitude, the two objects then moved southeast and quickly disappeared. Rather strange and atypical, this sighting cannot be definitively concluded due to its limited evidence, which stems primarily from the brief statement given to the National Gendarmerie. The Gendarmerie was unable to conduct a more thorough investigation. A field investigation, more than two years after the event, would likely yield little new information. This case is classified as Class C.

summary: Witness observation of the movement of a white glow in the sky followed by another luminous object: lack of information.
description: On the evening of July 16, 2010, at 11:30 PM, two people observed two luminous phenomena in the sky. Only one witness reported seeing a very bright white glow, similar to a large star, moving rapidly toward the northwest. After a minute, it faded and disappeared. Intrigued, this witness decided to get binoculars, and upon returning, observed the movement of a circular luminous phenomenon. Accelerations and oscillations were observed as the object moved away and disappeared. While of relatively low strangeness, this observation has many characteristics of a satellite transit. However, due to a lack of precise information (exact time, archives of satellite transit reports for 2010) to validate this hypothesis, this case is classified as Class C.

summary: Successive observations of Venus.
description: A witness reported observing a luminous phenomenon on July 15, 16, and 17, 2010, which appeared around 10:00 PM and disappeared around 11:10 PM. Other people present did not provide testimony. The main witness took photographs of the phenomenon. Reconstructing the direction of observation shows a center pointing westward. The characteristics described by the witness (a very bright point of light in the sky, observed for several consecutive days in the same location for extended periods (up to 60 minutes), descending toward the horizon) leave no doubt as to the observation of a celestial object. The planet Venus, with a magnitude of -4.1, was located in the observed portion of the sky. The event is classified as Class A, as is the observation of the planet Venus.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On July 13, 2010, at 11:27 PM, a witness observed three orange lights arranged in a triangle in the sky, approximately 150 meters away, outlining a dark mass. Initially stationary, the object then moved slowly in a linear motion without any noise. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. The characteristics of the observation resemble those of a well-known and frequently observed phenomenon: the passage of Thai lanterns (the festive period for observation is in July, specifically the night of July 13-14; the observation of three orange lights was silent; the objects moved linearly in the same direction; and the wind direction was roughly consistent with the observation, given that it was made by the sea, where local winds vary with the terrain). The dark triangular shape between the three lights described by the witness is a known phenomenon suggested by the human brain. The sighting presents no unusual features. The case is weak due to the single witness statement (despite the large crowd that must have been outside at the time) and the limited information contained in the police report. The plausible hypothesis of observing Thai lanterns passing by is retained, and this case, with its low level of unusualness, is classified as Class B, as most likely explained.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On July 10, 2010, at 2:30 a.m., a witness and his wife observed between 15 and 20 luminous orange orbs in the sky. They moved silently along a south-north trajectory. The observation lasted fifteen minutes, during which the witness took photographs. No other witness statements were collected by the police. The witness's photographs leave no doubt as to the highly probable observation of sky lanterns.

summary: Observation of the movement of Thai lanterns.
description: A witness reported seeing streaks followed by several red-orange discs moving silently across the sky on July 11, 2010, at approximately 2:20 AM. The witness took photographs during the observation, which lasted about 15 to 20 minutes. The "red discs" photographed by the witness correspond to the zoom level used during the photography. The described characteristics (several waves of red-orange light moving in the same direction) largely correspond to those of known phenomena such as sky lanterns. This hypothesis is supported by the discovery by the village mayor of partially burned lanterns in the town hall parking lot. This case is classified as Class A, like the observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the rapid, straight and silent movement of a bright white oval ball: lack of information.
description: On July 9, 2010, around 10:00 PM, two witnesses observed a bright, white, oval-shaped ball in the sky, flying at high speed along a straight trajectory. No sound was heard; the object disappeared to the north. The witness took a photograph and contacted the local press. Several hypotheses were considered for this somewhat strange phenomenon of a luminous spot moving in a straight line from south to north. A fireball would have been much faster and would have produced a trail; the International Space Station (ISS), visible in the French sky that evening, was not moving in that direction and appeared as a very bright point, not as a "plate." The passage of a metallic party balloon, drifting with the wind (10th, 20 km/h), still exposed to the sun because it was higher in the sky (sunset at 9:20 PM), could explain this observation, but its apparent speed would have been lower (due to much stronger high-altitude winds). Given this uncertainty, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C," a moderately unusual case of average consistency.

summary: Nighttime observation outdoors of the movement of a red teche growing larger in the shape of a blinking ball: lack of information.
description: During an outdoor reception on July 8, 2010, at 11:00 PM, about twenty people spotted a red luminous phenomenon. One witness reported seeing a red lantern that grew larger and larger, resembling a flashing red ball surrounded by a mauve-violet ring. It moved silently and in a straight line at a constant speed. The object's sudden disappearance ended the observation. Only one witness account was collected. While of moderate strangeness, the evidence is weak given the lack of precise coordinates for the observation site and the limited information regarding the phenomenon's direction (initially recorded westward, then from the Bauges massif towards Mont Granier, corresponding to a south-southwest axis that barely passed directly over Barberaz). Therefore, we cannot confirm the Thai lantern hypothesis.

summary: Observation of the rectilinear movement of a bright light in the sky: passage of the ISS.
description: An intriguing witness reported his observation: on July 6, 2010, at approximately 11:40 PM, he observed, for less than two minutes, a bright light moving rapidly eastward. The trajectory was straight. Due to the witness's precise description, this observation, of low oddity and good consistency, is almost certainly due to the passage of the ISS. This case is classified as Class A.

summary: Observation by a witness of the straight passage OE of a light: probable observation of the passage of the international space station.
description: During the night of July 4-5, 2010, at approximately 12:15 a.m., a witness observed a very bright light passing in a straight line (OE) from their bedroom window. The object disappeared, obscured by the roof. Although the ISS was not visible from the observation point until 12:23 a.m. (legal time), we consider the 7-minute margin of error relative to the time reported by the witness to be acceptable, given that they themselves indicated +/- 12:15 a.m. This case is classified as Class B, meaning a very probable sighting of the International Space Station.

summary: posteriori observation on a film of details not noticed during filming.
description: On July 4, 2010, a witness filmed a beach from his vehicle parked facing the sea. The next day, he discovered details in his video that he hadn't seen when he filmed the previous day. The witness did not want his video to be posted online. The video and photos he submitted contained a mix of standard details (poor quality video taken with a mobile phone, partly through a car windshield facing the sun, resulting in multiple reflections and artifacts; a very blurry, dark area that could be attributed to an insect near the lens; various traces of aircraft afterburners). Furthermore, the witness saw nothing on site and did not describe any particular phenomenon requiring analysis, but rather several phenomena and trajectories that were "assumed" after the fact. These "observations," lacking any degree of strangeness, are classified as C because they are unusable.

summary: Observation of the movements of a bright white point in the sky: passage of the ISS and probable satellites.
description: On July 3, 2010, starting at 11:50 PM, a witness observed the movement of a bright white point in the sky, which intrigued them. No unusual noises were heard during the filmed observation. Of low strangeness and moderate consistency (single witness), this observation corresponds perfectly to the observation of the International Space Station (ISS) for its first part. The second and third parts described are likely observations of unidentified satellites. This case is classified as Class A: observation of the International Space Station (ISS).

summary: Observation of the silent passage of a luminous orange object across the sky.
description: On July 3, 2010, at 3:13 a.m., a witness observed a flame-red object between two clouds. The object, initially motionless, then moved silently southward before disappearing. The characteristics of the sighting resemble those of a well-known and frequently observed phenomenon: Thai lanterns (the sighting occurred during the festive period in July, on Saturday night into Sunday morning, near a festive location such as a hotel hosting weddings and offering bed and breakfast accommodations, and with an orange flame). According to weather records (Auxerre weather reports), the wind was light and unstable. The helical shape described by the witness could be explained by observing a flying lantern from below (see comparison image). The sighting itself was not unusual. The case is weak due to the single witness statement and the limited information contained in the police report. The plausible hypothesis of the observation of a Thai-type lantern is retained and this case of low level of strangeness is class B as very probably explained.

summary: Observation in the sky of the passage with sudden change of direction of luminous phenomena: flight of the Patrouille de France.
description: On July 2, 2010, starting at 10:45 PM and lasting for thirty minutes, three witnesses observed from a balcony the rapid movement and changes of direction of luminous phenomena in the sky passing over the town. A loud, propeller-like noise was heard during the observation. As is customary on the first Friday of July, the Patrouille de France (French Air Force aerobatic demonstration team) was conducting a night flight in the area (information confirmed by the CNOA - French Air Force Aerobatic Committee). The witness account corresponds quite well with this event.

summary: Probable sighting of an aircraft.
description: On July 1, 2010, around midnight, a witness observed a bright point moving in a distinctive chevron pattern in the sky. The unusual aspect of this case lies solely in the chevron shape of the movement. The witness reported a frequency of approximately two seconds for this chevron pattern. By comparing this with a long-exposure photograph of a passenger plane (attached), where alternating red and white lights can be seen along the axis of movement, illuminated every second, GEIPAN hypothesizes that this flashing could have been interpreted by the witness as a chevron pattern. GEIPAN therefore classifies this case as "B": probable observation of an aircraft.

summary: Probable observation of the ISS passing overhead.
description: On July 1, 2010, at around 11 p.m., a witness observed a luminous phenomenon moving from west to east. The movement was slow and at a constant speed, without any unusual noise. Predictions for the International Space Station's (ISS) passage had been calculated for a 2010 summer sky report on the GEIPAN website (/geipan/actualites/01072010-Ciel-dete-Attention-aux-meprises-.html). These predictions indicate that the witness likely observed the ISS passing overhead.

summary: 07.2010. Observation of the rapid passage of a rectangular object of aluminium colour at very high altitude: lack of information.
description: Between July 1st and 12th, 2010, around 11:00 AM, a witness observed a rectangular, aluminum-colored object rapidly passing in the sky for a few seconds. No sound was heard during the observation. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. This sighting is very strange, but the testimony is very inconsistent: only one witness despite a densely populated area, a very short observation of a few seconds, and no precise date. The witness's sincerity is not in question, but a temporary vision problem (glare) cannot be ruled out. It is not possible to conduct a thorough investigation into this case. GEIPAN classifies it as case "C" due to a lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of the stationary presence then the movement of a black point in the sky: lack of information.
description: On Wednesday, June 30, 2010, at approximately 5:15 PM, a witness was intrigued by the presence of a large, stationary black dot in the sky. This dot then moved and disappeared behind a cloud. While of moderate strangeness and good consistency despite a lack of orientation, this observation of a large black dot cannot be concluded at this stage; further investigation of the various hypotheses is no longer possible. Unfortunately, the one-month delay after the questionnaire was received makes it impossible to obtain the radar recordings. This case is classified as Class C due to a lack of independent witness statements and corroborating evidence.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On June 26, 2010, at approximately 12:10 a.m., a witness observed two bright yellow-orange lights. They crossed the sky from east to west at a constant speed. They disappeared into the urban landscape. Two other people reportedly saw this phenomenon, but no further accounts were collected. Based on the witness's description, he likely observed Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation by a pilot of the rectilinear movement of a very bright point towards the South: no trace of smoke or fuel: observation of the International Space Station (ISS).
description: On June 27, 2010, at 6:05 PM, a pilot and co-pilot flying from Noumea to Seoul in an Airbus A330, at an altitude of 40,000 feet (12,500 meters), spotted a very bright light pointing towards the 3 o'clock position. This light was moving rapidly along a straight trajectory oriented southeast. No smoke or signs of combustion were observed. The speed was estimated at Mach 6 at an altitude of at least 80,000 feet (approximately 25,000 meters). As the light point approached the 3 o'clock position (90° to the right), the pilot contacted air traffic control based in Guam, without providing a precise position or heading. The controller, initially surprised, replied in the negative before contacting an American Airlines flight in the area a minute later to request confirmation of any unreported air traffic. The crew of the American Airlines flight confirmed the sighting. The observation ended after 5 minutes, when the bright point passed into the blind spot of the flight crew. Only one witness statement was collected. This sighting has all the characteristics of a satellite sighting; the most likely hypothesis is the International Space Station (ISS). The indications of position in the sky, date, time, and duration of the sighting are consistent with the proposed hypothesis. As always in these cases, the distance and speed estimates made by the witness, even an experienced pilot, cannot be accurate. Without reference points, it is absolutely impossible for a witness to estimate the distance, size, and speed of an unfamiliar object. Only the angular velocity of the phenomenon's movement can be considered precisely. Since the ISS is much brighter than other satellites, the crews would have perceived it as closer and at a lower altitude. The information regarding the position in the sky, date, time, and duration of the observation was accurately recorded and is consistent with the proposed hypothesis (see the detailed investigation report). GEIPAN classifies this case as A: observation of the International Space Station (ISS).

summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous orange object and sudden loss of altitude and brightness: lack of information.
description: In the early hours of Saturday, June 26, 2010, around 1:00 AM, eight people observed a very bright orange sphere moving silently at low altitude and constant speed in the Parisian sky. The sphere then suddenly dropped sharply in altitude and brightness. Only one witness account was reported to GEIPAN (the French National Gendarmerie's Office for the Study and Observation of Unidentified Flying Objects). Due to the lack of independent witnesses and the absence of any further evidence, this observation cannot be definitively confirmed, although a strong suspicion of a flying lantern remains. This case is classified as Class C due to the lack of independent witnesses and corroborating evidence to validate or refute the flying lantern hypothesis.

summary: Probable observation of the ISS (International Space Station) passing overhead.
description: On Friday, June 25, 2010, at 12:50 a.m., a witness observed a luminous phenomenon from their terrace that intrigued them. For one to two minutes, this person followed the silent movement of a very bright, spherical white glow. The investigation, entrusted to a National Police Inspectorate (IPN), determined that the witness had likely followed the passage of the International Space Station.

summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous spherical object: passage of the ISS.
description: On June 25, 2010, at 11:40 PM, a witness observed a bright, spherical object in the sky, which intrigued them. The object moved from west to east, passing over their home. The witness most likely observed the International Space Station (ISS), which crossed the sky from west-southwest to east, passing almost directly overhead between 11:34 PM and 11:38 PM. This is a Class A case: ISS sighting.

summary: Observing the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On June 20, 2010, at approximately 12:30 a.m., witnesses observed three luminous red-orange spheres in the sky. These spheres were moving in a northwesterly direction. The characteristics of the observation made by three witnesses (Saturday night/Sunday morning around midnight, three orange spheres moving in the same direction, silently and at low altitude) correspond to a flight of Thai lanterns. This hypothesis was also considered by one of the witnesses. The north-northwest wind direction also corresponds to the direction of movement described in the observation.

summary: Prolonged observation of a red light and a luminous object in the night: lack of information.
description: On Saturday, June 19, 2010, at approximately 11:30 PM, a witness near a village festival was intrigued by a red light that varied in intensity and by an object with white lights that the witness did not recognize. The observation lasted between 5 and 10 minutes. The witness initially thought it might be one or more helicopters, as the lights remained stationary throughout, but the absence of noise and the slow, atypical flashing of the lights did not fit this hypothesis. A tethered balloon equipped with lights could also explain the observation, especially if it was part of the fireworks display that was also observed. Unfortunately, we were unable to verify this second hypothesis. A few balloons at altitude, illuminated by the last rays of the sun, which had set a little over an hour earlier, could have produced a similar spectacle. While of moderate strangeness due to the static nature and the rhythmic pulsing of the UFO's light, and of good consistency thanks to a precise description from the witness, this observation cannot unfortunately be definitively concluded without further investigation. This case is classified as Class C due to a lack of independent testimonies and corroborating evidence.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of several luminous orange balls: probable observation of Thai lanterns.
description: On June 13, 2010, at 1:00 AM, a witness saw luminous orange orbs gradually appear in the sky. The witness counted between 15 and 20 orbs moving quickly and silently before fading away as they rose into the air. The witness's description perfectly matches the observation of a lecher of Thai lanterns: orange color, smooth and silent movement with the wind (from northeast to southwest, see weather report), and disappearance after a few minutes. Furthermore, the time and day (1:00 AM on a Sunday in June) are common for this type of event. This case is classified as "B": probable observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Presence of a black triangular object at high altitude: probable observation of a balloon (weather or child's toy).
description: On June 12, 2010, between 2:00 and 2:30 PM, several people gathered around a barbecue noticed a black, triangular object in the sky at a high altitude. The object appeared stationary, then began to ascend before disappearing behind a cloud. There was a north-northwest wind that day. The witness was observing from the north-northwest, that is, facing the wind: a balloon in its ascending phase, following the wind, would therefore appear relatively immobile to the observer. The triangular shape of the object suggests a torahedral balloon, black because it was seen against the sun at its zenith. This balloon could be a weather balloon launched from Blagnac or by Météo-France, or even a toy balloon released in the city center (numerous end-of-year celebrations were taking place in Toulouse that day). The movement, color, and shape of the object are consistent with a balloon filled with hydrogen or helium and carried by the wind. This case is class "B," a probable observation of a balloon.

summary: Probable sightings of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On June 12, 2010, starting at 11:30 PM, several residents of Calais observed about ten luminous orange and white orbs in the sky from different locations. They appeared to originate from the same place and moved slowly and silently along an upward trajectory before disappearing. An article in the local newspaper on August 17, 2010, reported a witness who claimed to have seen a lantern release in front of the Detroit high school, but no such testimony was collected by the police. These individuals likely observed the passage of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of a point of light.
description: On June 10, 2010, between 10:30 PM and 11:00 PM, a witness observed a bright light from their terrace that intrigued them. It remained stationary to the southeast for approximately 15 minutes before moving northeast and disappearing, hidden by the landscape. Following the police report, the investigations conducted by the Gendarmerie failed to re-establish contact with the main witness or the other identified witnesses. No rapid means of communication (telephone, email) allowed contact with the witness. Time has passed since the observation, and the information contained in the report does not allow for further investigation or the conduct of an inquiry. The duration (unverifiable) and the brief description of the phenomenon by a single witness leave the door open to all hypotheses (airplane in a holding pattern?, balloon with its payload underneath (circular shape with a plume below?), something else?). The case is class C due to lack of information.

summary: Probable observation of an aircraft passing overhead.
description: witness observed a luminous, stationary circular object in the airspace around 12:30 a.m. on June 7, 2010. The observation lasted approximately 15 seconds before the object rapidly disappeared without a sound. Following further information received from SNA-Ouest on December 7, 2010, this observation likely corresponds to the approach/landing phase of an aircraft at Nantes Airport (a commercial flight that landed at 12:37 a.m. local time). The landing light was described as a "bright white luminous sphere" "surrounded by flashes" (wing lights).

summary: Observation of the silent passage of a luminous yellow ball in the sky: lack of information.
description: On Saturday, June 5, 2010, around midnight, a witness observed a luminous yellow sphere surrounded by an orange halo passing silently for 5 to 6 seconds. Its trajectory was north-south. The described phenomenon strongly resembles a Thai lantern, which can be purchased in various colors. The fireworks observed by the witness also suggest that the night was an occasion for various festivities. The linear trajectory is characteristic of this type of observation; however, the wind was blowing from the north at midnight (measured at the airport), which does not allow for confirmation of the lantern hypothesis. Nevertheless, in mountainous areas, with light winds, local breezes can be oriented differently from one valley to another. While not particularly unusual, this observation, with its relatively good consistency and accurate account of events, possesses many characteristics of a Thames lantern. However, the lack of local wind data prevents confirmation of this hypothesis. This case is classified as Class C due to the absence of precise weather data, independent eyewitness accounts, and corroborating evidence.

summary: Observation of the very high-speed movement of a point of light along a straight trajectory: lack of information.
description: On the night of Saturday, June 5th to Sunday, June 6th, 2010, several witnesses were intrigued by the rapid passage of a white light. Its trajectory was low and from east to south. The observation lasted between 5 and 10 seconds. A large satellite could have produced this appearance (apart from the visible shape, which may be a kind of optical illusion). Some satellites are in slightly retrograde orbits (inclination on the order of 1/100th) which could follow an east-to-south trajectory. When GEIPAN conducted this investigation (in 2012), simulations were no longer possible for a date in 2010. We cannot definitively conclude that this observation, while relatively minor (a point of light moving in a straight line) and consistent (precise witness testimony), is a Class C case. Due to a lack of independent and corroborating witness accounts, this case is classified as Class C.

summary: Probable sighting of a Thai lantern passing overhead.
description: witness observed an unusual phenomenon from their balcony on the night of June 5-6, 2010, at 12:37 a.m. A white, rectangular light, originating from the mountains above Ajaccio, crossed the bay at very high speed, without making any noise and following a straight trajectory. The characteristics of the observation (Saturday/Sunday night shortly after midnight, non-glaring white light, no noise, trajectory consistent with the wind direction) suggest a luminous balloon of the Thai lantern type.

summary: Observation of the movement of flying lanterns.
description: On June 5, 2010, at approximately 11:55 PM, numerous witnesses observed a column of orange balls moving. The single questionnaire and the described characteristics of the observation led the investigation to believe that Thai lanterns were being seen. Contacted by GEIPAN (the French National Group for the Study and Protection of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena), the Communications Department of the Tournan-en-Brie town hall confirmed this suspicion, specifying that a wedding had taken place in their town with a Thai lantern release on Saturday, June 5, at midnight.

summary: Observations of the movement of Thai lanterns.
description: A witness observed, for a few seconds around 11:00 PM, the silent, straight movement of a luminous phenomenon composed of five white and yellow halos towards the northwest. Following the classification and publication of the case from Tournan-en-Brie (77) on the same date, the witness contacted GEIPAN and believes his observation could correspond to the same phenomenon: a lantern release. Another witness reported a similar sighting from Île Saint-Louis between 10:50 PM and 11:13 PM, also on June 5, 2010. This case is classified as Category A.

summary: Probable sighting of flying lanterns.
description: On June 4, 2010, at 11:15 PM, a witness observed three luminous points in the sky for two to three minutes. Stationary and of the same size, they all disappeared simultaneously. The witness declined to give a statement to the police, and no other statements were collected regarding this phenomenon. The description of the phenomenon (the successive appearance of one, then three luminous points) suggests, once again, the observation of sky lanterns appearing successively in the sky and then disappearing (as the witness described them). The weather report at midnight from the Montpellier station indicated a light northerly wind, consistent with the trajectory of a light object described by the witness. The observed phenomenon had a low degree of strangeness. The hypothesis of sky lanterns being observed is the most likely.

summary: Probable sighting of a Thai lantern passing overhead.
description: On June 4, 2010, at 11:12 PM, a witness filmed an orange light passing across the sky. A second witness, who took photographs but was unable to provide them to investigators, described the phenomenon as "a kind of balloon containing a sort of lantern inside." The main witness was interviewed by the police four months after the sighting. The video attached to the police report clearly shows a Thai-style lantern in flight. The origin and launch site were not determined.

summary: Probable observation of the movement of a balloon (weather or other).
