description: On June 3, 2010, at 7:28 a.m., a witness observed a white sphere passing across the sky for about ten seconds. Small in size and flying above buildings, this object quickly disappeared and was hidden by the urban landscape. No noise was heard during the observation. No other reports were collected regarding this phenomenon. The witness did not wish to file a report with the police. The description of the observation, detailed in the questionnaire submitted to GEIPAN by the main witness, clearly suggests the observation of an object lighter than air (a weather balloon or similar). The weather conditions at Roissy Airport at the time of the observation indicated a light northerly wind (between 360° and 10°), consistent with the north-south trajectory described by the witness.

summary: Observation of a ball of light: iridium flash.
description: witness observed a ball of light in the sky around 12:45 a.m. on June 3, 2010, which intrigued him. This stationary object gradually dimmed, and the witness lost sight of it. No noise was noticed during the 15-20 second observation. Following the publication of cases categorized as "C," an internet user reported the possibility of an Iridium flare to GEIPAN (the French UFO research group). GEIPAN investigated this hypothesis. The witness's description corresponds to the observation of a flare from an Iridium satellite, a rare and spectacular phenomenon that occurred at that time, was visible from that location, and could not have escaped the observer who was looking in that direction. However, the witness did not provide information about the elevation (site) of the phenomenon in the sky. This UFO observation is classified as Ae, for Iridium flares.

summary: Probable atmospheric reentry of a meteor.
description: On June 2, 2010, at approximately 8:30-8:45 PM, a witness briefly observed the passage of an ovoid-shaped object with a fluorescent pale green color. This luminous object originated in the south and moved north-northeast along a straight trajectory at high speed. No sound was heard, and no trail was observed behind the object. The observation describes a luminous phenomenon lasting a very short time (1 to 2 seconds), very fast, with a comet-like shape (suggesting atmospheric reentry), and a fluorescent pale green color (also characteristic of atmospheric reentry). This case is classified as a B incident, indicating a probable atmospheric reentry of a meteor.

summary: Observation of the movement of about twenty orange balls in the same direction.
description: On May 30, 2010, at 10:50 PM, two people observed approximately twenty orange orbs passing over their home. These orbs moved silently in the same direction. The witness did not respond to repeated requests from GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) for further information. Without a police report or additional information, any investigation is impossible. Even though the characteristics (several orange orbs following a simultaneous transverse trajectory) suggest the known phenomenon of sky lanterns flying in formation, this case is classified as Category C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation in the sky of a very bright yellow point: astronomical observation of Venus.
description: On Monday, May 24, 2010, at 10:30 PM, a witness observed a very bright, stationary yellow point from the first floor of a house. He alerted his parents, who observed the same thing. Two photographs were taken with a digital camera. No unusual noises were heard during the observation, which lasted 45 minutes before the witness decided to go to bed. The witness was intrigued because he also reported other observations of luminous phenomena from this house, without giving precise dates and in a different geographical area. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. The observation of May 24, 2010, was certainly that of Venus. The other repeated observations were probably of other celestial bodies (Mars and Sirius), which were very visible in April in the Southwest (see the star chart for April 2010). The three bright spots observed through binoculars are likely an optical aberration or an effect of atmospheric turbulence: this effect is very common when observing very bright celestial bodies. Witnesses also observed weather balloons regularly launched from the Météo France center in Trappes (12 km southeast of the observation site) during the day or early evening. These balloons are sometimes launched in groups and are likely to suddenly disappear when, at high altitude, the sun disappears below the horizon. This case of May 24, 2010, is classified as "A": an astronomical observation of Venus.

summary: Successive observations on the same evening of the silent movement of an oblong object in the sky: lack of information.
description: On Sunday, May 23, 2010, at approximately 10:35 PM, a witness on their 6th-floor balcony was intrigued by an unusual object in the Parisian sky. The object "whirled" silently and without lights and was seen again at 10:41 PM. No other reports were collected. The whirling shape described by the witness could hardly be a balloon; a visual defect (phosphene, floater) remains a possibility but impossible to prove. Of low to moderate strangeness, but lacking sufficient consistency due to the noted meteorological inconsistencies, this observation cannot be concluded in the absence of further data. This case is classified as "C" due to the lack of independent or corroborating reports.

summary: Probable sighting of a Thai lantern passing overhead.
description: On May 23, 2010, at approximately 10:45 PM, several people observed an orange light moving in the sky. It moved horizontally, then hovered before moving vertically and disappearing over the horizon. No sound was heard during the five-minute observation. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. These individuals likely witnessed the passage of a Thai lantern.

summary: Probable trace of an insect passing through during the taking of a photograph.
description: On May 22, 2010, at 1:54 PM, a person took photos of a child. Later, they noticed a strange object in one of the photographs, which had gone unnoticed when the picture was taken. The witness filed a police report, which was received late by GEIPAN (the French National Group for the Study and Protection of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena). The initial police investigation and inquiries into air traffic and the surrounding area did not allow them to determine the nature of the object, which only the witness had photographed. Finally, an analysis of the photograph sent by the witness convinced GEIPAN that it was an insect very close to the lens, which is consistent with the shutter speed and the focus on the closest subject (the child on the motorcycle). To be so blurry under those shooting conditions, the object must have been at a distance less than the hyperfocal distance, therefore well under 1 meter. Given the camera's specifications and settings, it can be verified that if the object measured 1 cm, it would have been 13 cm from the lens, which is consistent with the size of a winged insect. The lighting of this "insect-like object" is also consistent with sunlight. This case falls into the category of observations made on one of the many media (photos or videos) received by GEIPAN: while not a direct visual observation at the time of capture, the observation is made during subsequent viewing on a computer screen. The case is classified as Class B, meaning it likely captures an insect very close to the camera.

summary: Successive observations of a scintillating bar with spots: astronomical observation of Venus.
description: Two witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky over several consecutive evenings, in the direction of the west-northwest. This fixed light slowly set. They took photographs. The strangeness of this observation lies not in the phenomenon itself, but in the witnesses' interpretation of it, based on the shape of the line they saw and the photograph taken from the ground floor. Indeed, the object observed in the sky had all the characteristics of the planet Venus. The photograph taken from the ground is indeed strange at first glance; however, the witness photographed a lamppost, not Venus. Once down to the ground floor, Venus was hidden by the wooded hill, and only the light from the streetlights reached it through the foliage. This case is Class A: repeated observations of the planet Venus, and a photographic error involving a lamppost seen through foliage.

summary: Observations of a falling, burning object. Lack of information.
description: On May 17, 2010, at approximately 9:45 PM, a couple observed a burning triangular object slowly descending in the sky. The main witness initially thought it was a flaming ultralight aircraft crashing. Another object, forming a torch, detached from this object. No other witness statements were collected. Given the extensive search conducted by the gendarmerie, the ultralight aircraft crash hypothesis can be ruled out. The possibility of a misinterpretation as falling space debris is then considered (the appearance and duration of the observation could be consistent). A piece of debris was reported to have re-entered the atmosphere that day (29569 DELTA 4 DEB), but its 98° orbital inclination does not correspond to the observation (which was directed E-NE); this hypothesis cannot be confirmed. GEIPAN classifies this case as "C": insufficient information to draw a conclusion.

summary: Observation of the movement of bright points in the sky: lack of information.
description: The witness observed a bright point in the starry sky, accompanied by a red point to its right, below which was a green point. These points of light moved together, resembling an airplane, until they separated and moved in opposite directions. The beginning of the observation (a bright point above the horizon, with red and green points) is entirely consistent with the perception of a star or planet with atmospheric twinkling. The second part of the testimony ("the two points separated, each moving in an opposite direction") does not correspond to any known phenomenon, except perhaps an optical illusion following the disappearance of the object. With a low degree of strangeness at the beginning of the observation and a moderate degree at the end, and weak consistency (single witness, inconsistencies and imprecision in the testimony), this case of observation cannot be concluded due to a lack of reliable information or corroboration. This case is classified as Class C.

summary: Probable sighting of Thai lanterns.
description: A witness observed, for a few seconds at 3:20 a.m. on May 2, 2010, a very bright sphere moving rapidly in a southeasterly direction before suddenly disappearing. A few seconds later, a second sphere appeared and then disappeared, completing a 180-degree loop downwards. The description of observing a bright sphere suddenly disappearing, followed by a second bright sphere disappearing in turn (extinguishing due to fuel exhaustion), suggests the observation of luminous sky lanterns, especially since the observation occurred during the night from Saturday to Sunday. However, despite repeated requests from GEIPAN (the French UFO research group), no further information has been obtained to allow for a more thorough investigation. The case is classified as Class B, indicating a probable sky lantern sighting.

summary: Sighting of a black dot in the sky: probable sighting of a balloon.
description: On May 1, 2010, at 5:00 PM, several people observed a black dot in the sky from an apartment. Initially stationary, the dot moved silently. The black dot was filmed by one of the witnesses. The testimony strongly suggests a lighter-than-air craft, more or less following the local wind (appearing in the west, disappearing towards the south). It should be noted that the wind patterns that day seemed unsettled and complex: northerly wind in Lyon, no wind in Grenoble, and westerly wind in Geneva. The precise wind direction in Sallanches could not be determined. A local hot air balloon association was consulted: no flights were scheduled at that time. It could have been a helium balloon launched, or lost, by a private individual, or even an experimental airship. GEIPAN (the French National Center for Experimental and Explosive Activities) did not observe any green reflections on the object in the video. This case, ultimately not very strange, is class "B": probable observation of a balloon (balloon not identified by GEIPAN)

summary: Observation of Venus.
description: On April 29, 2010, at 11:00 PM, three people, during their professional maritime surveillance duties, observed the movement of a luminous phenomenon in the sky. The observation was made facing the sea from the footbridge of a tower overlooking the ocean. Photographs were taken, notably through a telescope. The majority of the described characteristics of the phenomenon correspond to those known for a planetary motion (trajectory, speed, duration) and a strong luminosity from a single point near an artificial light source, such as the planet Venus. The strangeness of the observed phenomenon is low. The confirmation by three witnesses of the duration of the phenomenon, its description and trajectory, and its presence in a very precise area of the sky lends considerable weight to the case. The verification of the presence of the planet Venus in the observation area throughout the entire observation period is a certain and well-verified hypothesis.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On April 24, 2010, at approximately 11:30 PM, two people observed about thirty lights in the sky, all moving in the same direction without any sound being heard. Their number decreased over the course of several minutes, and they eventually disappeared completely. The witness, who filmed the observation, concluded after some research that they were Thai lanterns. No other reports were collected regarding the appearance or origin of these flying lanterns. Based on the description provided, these individuals likely observed Thai lanterns.

summary: Probable observation of an atmospheric reentry of a bolide.
description: In the early hours of April 17, 2010, at 1:10 a.m., near Bourg-en-Bresse, a driver and her daughter observed a very rapid flash across the sky. During its descent, a green ball split in two and then disappeared. Based on the information gathered (questionnaire, drawing, and photograph of the view from inside the car), they likely witnessed the atmospheric reentry of a meteor. This fireball was observed and photographed by the amateur meteor observatory in Chaligny (south of Nancy), part of the BOAM network (Amateur Meteor Observation Database). The description (precise date and time of observation, direction, green light characteristic of atmospheric ionization, movement and trajectory at high altitude appearing "parallel" to the horizon, distance greater than 100 kms) and the drawings of the observation by the witness correspond well to the recording of the bolide made by the BOAM station.

summary: Observation of the star Sirius.
description: On April 14, 2010, a witness observed an intriguing phenomenon in the sky. Between 10 p.m. and midnight, looking south, he saw a luminous object with varying colors. He filmed part of his observation. No unusual noises were heard. The investigation determined that the witness had made an astronomical observation of the star Sirius (see the investigation report).

summary: Observation of the slow movement of a red point of light.
description: witness reported seeing a slowly moving red light on April 14, 2010, between 9:50 PM and 9:56 PM. The characteristics of the observation—a red light moving slowly upward, becoming stationary, and then disappearing—are reminiscent of the (now well-known) lecher of a Thai-style sky lantern. Unfortunately, the additional information requested by GEIPAN from the main witness (a police report that would have allowed for a preliminary investigation) was not followed up. The case is classified as Class C due to lack of information.

summary: Observations by several flight crews of the presence of a light with color variations: very likely observations of the planet Venus on the horizon.
description: On April 14, 2010, at 10:44 PM, a total of five commercial flight crews observed a bright point of variable color in the sky in a west-northwest direction. The analysis conducted and the hypotheses proposed lead us to divide the conclusion into two groups: - for flights RYR57ZB and RAM697, flying approximately north of the other three (roughly between La Rochelle and Limoges), the observation appears very consistent, with a misinterpretation due to Venus, which was clearly visible to their side. - for flights RYR8CW, RYR7CT, and EIN577, flying east of Bordeaux, the question of Venus's visibility arises, given a possible obstruction by the aircraft's nose. The presence of a short radar trace, difficult to interpret, could lead to the conclusion of an unknown object, but the evidence remains too weak in the absence of detailed accounts from the various crews. The observed twinkling in several colors is due to the dispersion of Venus's light passing through the different layers of the atmosphere and varying according to their fluctuations, combined with the rapid movement of the aircraft in cruise flight and the Earth's rotation. This case initially had a high degree of strangeness, but ultimately proved to be moderate. Its consistency is very good, due to the numerous, albeit very brief, accounts. GEIPAN classifies this case as B: highly probable observations of the planet Venus on the horizon.

summary: Observations of the silent movement of bright red lights at low altitude: probable observation of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On Saturday, April 10, 2010, between 9:00 PM and 11:00 PM, several people observed two bright red lights moving silently across the sky at low altitude, following a straight north-south trajectory. These observations have all the characteristics of a Thai lantern display: color, duration, and movement with the wind. This is a Class B case, highly probable Thai lantern sighting.

summary: Observation of the movement of a bright white/yellow sphere in the sky: passage of the ISS.
description: witness reported on November 15, 2011, an observation made on April 10, 2010, at 6:23 a.m., of a luminous white/yellow sphere passing over a neighboring residence. After 5 seconds, the witness observed the sphere moving slowly and in a straight line toward another residence before rapidly disappearing, rising silently into the sky. The witness's description suggested an airplane seen head-on, with its runway lights on, but the object observed was silent, and the witness, who regularly observes the sky at that time of day, did not recognize it as an airplane. This case was initially classified as Class C due to a lack of information. Following a report from an internet user who suggested the possibility of an ISS pass, GEIPAN confirmed this hypothesis: the International Space Station (ISS) passed along this exact trajectory at that time (see the Calsky screenshot in the investigation materials). The file is class "A": ISS observation.

summary: Observation of the passage of an object with a red light at high altitude.
description: On April 9, 2010, at approximately 10:08 PM, a witness observed a very rapid, high-altitude passage of an object with a red light that diminished in intensity as it moved away. The object was quickly obscured by the landscape. The witness did not respond to repeated requests from GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) for further information. Without a police report or additional information, any investigation is impossible. The case is classified as C due to lack of information.

summary: Observations of Venus.
description: witness observed a bright point in the sky between 9:30 PM and 10:30 PM on April 7th and 9th, 2010. He filmed this point, whose color varied. The astronomical configuration of the sky at the date and time of the observation shows the planet Venus (magnitude -3.9, easily visible to the naked eye) in the observed sector of the sky (at 1/280th of a second at 9:30 PM local time). The observation was made several days in a row, and the witness recalls having observed the same phenomenon at the same time the previous year. The color changes described by the witness are due to optical effects (variations in brightness) during the recording of the video with the witness's camera.

summary: Observation of 3 luminous red-orange balls detaching themselves from an intense elongated light; sudden disappearance: lack of information.
description: On April 5, 2010, at 3:49 or 5:49 AM, a witness observed a very bright, elongated, and stationary white light from their balcony. They then noticed three luminous orbs, yellow and red in color, separate from the light and move in different directions. The main light suddenly disappeared. Only one witness statement was collected. The description (appearance of the luminous points, weekend night) could correspond to Thai lanterns. The "cigar" element, however, is more difficult to explain with the limited information provided. Further investigation and exploration of the possibilities (for example, clouds for cigars, position in the sky, conformity to the wind for balloons) would have required additional information that the witness never provided despite several requests. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the incident as category C: lack of information.

summary: Observation of the movement of a dark object in the sky: lack of information and cross-checking.
description: On March 31, 2010, at 6:20 PM, a person observed a dark-colored, shapeless object moving across the sky from their balcony. The witness had time to take photographs and called their wife. Only one witness statement was collected. This case of observing a distant object (estimated at 2 to 3 km), with erratic movement (see reconstruction from photos), presents a moderate degree of strangeness. The photographs provide sufficient evidence to support this case. The photographed object could correspond to numerous possibilities for a body moving in the air between the witness and the nuclear power plant: most likely a large bird, as the witness's wife initially perceived (see police report), a tethered balloon, a kite, a radio-controlled model... A tethered balloon could exhibit such behavior, given the strong wind that day (approximately 25 km/h). However, the object's disappearance into the clouds is inconsistent, unless the clouds obscured it. A helicopter is also a possibility, due to the heavy air traffic in this area (see police report), but the photographed shape is not a perfect match. The object's dynamic behavior is not unusual: it could be a bird or a kite, as the witnesses initially thought, or a tethered balloon or a helicopter. Verification of these multiple hypotheses is no longer possible. This case, consistent but not particularly strange, is classified as "C" due to a lack of additional information and corroboration.

summary: Observation of the passage of a luminous phenomenon with a trail: lack of information.
description: On March 30, 2010, at approximately 11:30 PM, a witness observed from their home the slow and silent northeastward movement of a luminous phenomenon beneath the clouds. The witness saw three luminous spheres with a trail behind them. No other witness accounts were collected. Due to the single witness's limited strangeness and lack of consistency, this observation remains unexplained for lack of information. A field investigation more than two years after the event would likely yield little additional information. This case is classified as C due to insufficient information.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On March 27, 2010, at 10:30 PM, two people observed from their homes the passage of about twenty luminous orbs that grouped together and then followed a west-east trajectory. The witnesses heard no noise. The characteristics of the observation (about twenty luminous orbs of yellow-orange color moving along the same trajectory for several minutes), as well as the photographs taken by a witness, correspond to the now well-known observation of a flight of Thai-type light lanterns. The date (Saturday evening) is also common for this type of observation (party, wedding, end of the weekend). The case is classified as Class B.

summary: Moon observation.
description: On March 17, 2010, at approximately 8:40 PM, a motorist observed an intriguing orange light phenomenon just above the horizon. He stopped and took photographs facing west just before the crescent-shaped phenomenon disappeared. The ephemerides for March 17, 2010 (and March 16) show that at 6:40 PM UTC (8:40 PM local time), the last phase of the new moon was just above the horizon, still illuminated by the sun and visible as a faint orange crescent (as photographed and described by the witness).

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On March 15, 2010, between 9:30 and 9:45 PM, a witness observed about ten luminous orbs passing across the sky. The characteristics of the formation described by the witness (orange luminous orbs moving in a uniform wave for several minutes before disappearing) describe a known phenomenon without any element of strangeness. The case is classified as UAP B, the probable sighting of flying lanterns.

summary: Observation of the movement of lights and a cylindrical shape.
description: While driving along the Thau Lagoon (34), a motorist observed two round lights passing overhead between 10:45 PM and 11:00 PM on March 11, 2010. He then distinguished a large, cigar-shaped mass moving quickly but silently at an altitude of 100 meters. No other witness statements were collected by the police. The witness also reported having witnessed several impressive sightings in the past. The level of strangeness of the observation was low (two lights moving at a relatively slow speed). The evidence gathered during the investigation did not allow for the confirmation or refutation of any possible interpretation, and the case remained insufficiently substantiated. The single witness statement could not be corroborated with other evidence, and the precise location of the phenomenon could not be determined due to the witness's unavailability. This case remains unexplained and inconsistent, without any unusual characteristics, it is class C.

summary: observation of the movement of orange balls.
description: On March 6, 2010, at approximately 11:05 PM, a driver and his passengers observed about fifteen reddish-orange orbs moving silently. A video was recorded on a cell phone during the observation, which lasted more than five minutes before the luminous orbs gradually disappeared. The driver's precise description closely resembled that of Thai lanterns released during festivals. Following the publication of a local newspaper article about this sighting, a person who had released 13 Thai lanterns came forward. The police investigation also concluded that the lanterns had been released during a private party located 2.5 km from the witnesses' observation site.

summary: Probable observation of lights related to festivities in Germany.
description: On March 4, 2010, around 8:30 p.m., a motorist spotted "suspicious" lights in the sky that she couldn't explain. She saw them several times afterward, always in the same location. It is likely that these lights were spotlights illuminating the numerous castles located on the mountain peaks to the east, in the Black Forest, on the other side of the Franco-German border. The period of the observation coincided with a festive time in France, but also in Germany, where very colorful celebrations (carnival-like festivals) take place at this time of year (Kappensitzung). Germans are very fond of these festivals.

summary: Observations by two people of the silent passage of an orange flying object: probable sighting of a Thai lantern.
description: Two people in their kitchen observed, for two minutes around 2:40 a.m. on February 28, 2010, the silent passage of a bright orange, shimmering sphere without any flashing. The object, at low altitude, moved along a straight trajectory and then disappeared vertically. This sighting leaves no doubt as to the authenticity of the testimonies, although they differed at the beginning of the investigation. The witnesses' account strongly suggests the passage of a Thai lantern. The impression of disappearing upwards is quite common when the lantern's flame goes out. The estimated direction of the object (NNE) is not entirely consistent with the wind direction (towards NNW), but firstly, the wind direction at ground level in Rivesaltes is not the same as at an altitude of 200 or 300 meters in Bages, and secondly, the direction estimate made by the witnesses is necessarily imprecise. The day and time (Saturday night to Sunday morning) are fairly common for lantern lechers, which are quite widespread in the region. This case is class "B": probable observation of a Thae lantern.

summary: Observing the sun.
description: On February 27, 2010, at 1:58 PM, a witness observed a curious luminous phenomenon in the direction of the southwest. A round, rainbow-colored glow and another white glow were observed for two minutes. No sound was heard. The witness took photographs. The characteristics of the observation described in the official report, as well as the two photographs taken by the witness, reveal no unusual features. They show separate cirrus clouds, well-known to meteorologists, in the form of filaments, mostly white in color. These clouds have a fibrous appearance and a silky sheen. The "flying objects" described and photographed by the witness correspond to the sun's southward movement through the cloud layer, hence the rainbow-colored light of the "second object" corresponds to the visible spectrum of sunlight.

summary: Astronomical observation of the star Sirius.
description: On February 22, 2010, at 1:55 a.m., a witness observed a stationary point of light from their garden, which intrigued them. Upon closer observation, they noticed that the light emitted by this point was of different colors. Impressed, the person called their brother, who confirmed the observation. The observation's duration, exceeding 20 minutes, clearly suggests the observation of a celestial phenomenon. The sky configuration at the time of the observation showed the star Sirius in the observed area. This star, the brightest in our sky, exhibits varying luminous aspects (as described by the witness). The case is classified as Class A, like the observation of the star Sirius.

summary: Sky lantern observation.
description: On the night of February 14, 2010, around midnight, numerous witnesses in the vicinity of Lorient observed the passage of luminous orbs. No sound was heard during these observations, which intrigued the witnesses. Several consistent accounts were reported to a major daily newspaper in western France and to GEIPAN (the French UFO research group). Following the publication of these accounts in the press, the owner of a Vietnamese restaurant reported having licked about thirty sky lanterns at midnight on the night of February 13-14, 2010, to celebrate the Chinese New Year with his guests. The time, launch location, and direction of travel of the event, which was filmed, perfectly match the accounts reported to GEIPAN.

summary: Probable observation of luminous effects from lasers.
description: From his car, a witness observed a luminous phenomenon on February 11, 2010, at 8:15 PM, consisting of three white lights rotating in the sky, appearing and disappearing successively. The phenomenon vanished abruptly. The observation of the three white lights rotating in the sky was made by a single witness who himself compared these lights to laser circles at a nightclub. The direction of observation corresponds to that of a nightclub that was scheduled to hold a "fluo night party" on February 12. A letter concerning possible laser tests or a laser show on February 11, 2010, was sent. In the absence of a response from the nightclub to this inquiry, this observation, without a police report, could be classified as a Class C incident due to lack of information. But the witness's deep conviction about the observation of a 'laser-type luminous phenomenon', without formal proof of this hypothesis being provided, allows this case to be classified as B, like the probable observation of laser circles.

summary: Observation of the rectilinear movement of a luminous phenomenon.
description: On February 7, 2010, at 4:33 a.m., a motorist on the A1 national highway, traveling from Lamentin to Fort-de-France (Martinique), observed what he described as a non-sparkling star over a distance of 300 meters. The phenomenon was at an estimated altitude of at least 700 meters. This light disappeared instantly at the end of the straight stretch of road. No unusual noise was heard during the 10-second observation. Among the hypotheses considered (plasma on a power line, reflection, meteor, eye strain), none could be confirmed or clearly ruled out. Given this uncertainty and the relatively minor nature of the case (it was ultimately just a distant point of light moving in a straight line), GEIPAN classified this case as Category C: Insufficient evidence to draw a conclusion. New evidence may emerge that either confirms or refutes one or the other of these hypotheses.

summary: Observation of the movement of a dark then luminous phenomenon: probable confusion with the sun.
description: witness reported to the gendarmerie and GEIPAN (the French National Center for Experimental and Perceived Objects) an observation of a luminous phenomenon made from his home on Wednesday, February 3, 2010, around 4:00 PM. The direction and elevation, according to the first reconstruction photograph, correspond exactly to the position of the Sun. It is therefore natural that the object was dazzling despite sunglasses, that it changed shape and color, and that indoor lighting appeared dim and pink or orange (QT pp. 2-4). Furthermore, the phenomenon disappeared with sunset (QT p. 15) behind the mountains. In this context, the second object described, whose position is given by the second photograph, could simply be a consequence of prolonged observation of the Sun, namely a phenomenon of retinal persistence. The witness mentions his neighbor, whom he contacted by telephone during the observation. The witness's account is ambiguous: he refers sometimes to a Sputnik, sometimes to a fireball, depending on whether one consults the official transcript or the Earth Questionnaire. The celestial bodies very low on the horizon are sometimes interpreted by witnesses as being much closer and at a low altitude. This case is classified as Class B, indicating probable confusion with the Sun, followed by glare after observing it.

summary: Observation in the cloudy sky of a large grey sphere with tubular features: lack of information
description: witness reported an observation made on January 21, 2010, at approximately 5:15 PM. While driving on National Route 524 towards Eauze, he spotted a dark gray, metallic-looking spherical object above a hill, seemingly composed of hexagons. The object appeared stationary but was oscillating from side to side. It disappeared instantly after 10 to 15 seconds of observation. No other witness statements were collected. This case is considered moderately to highly unusual due to the object's singular appearance and its instantaneous disappearance. However, given the imprecise location of the observation, the very short duration of the observation, and the single witness statement, this case is classified as moderately to weakly unusual. Due to a lack of information and corroboration, this case is classified as Class C.

summary: Observation of the slow movement of flashing white lights: probable observation of a train of weather balloons.
description: witness reported an observation made on January 21st between 7:42 and 7:45 AM: between the peaks of Grosse Tête and Grand Miceau, a group of flashing white lights moved slowly. The entire group disappeared, hidden by the landscape. The investigation revealed that a radiosonde launch using weather balloons had taken place near St. Exupéry Airport 1 hour and 40 minutes before the observation. The hypothesis that these balloons were illuminated by the rising sun remains the most plausible. This case is classified as Class B: probable observation of a train of weather balloons.

summary: Observation of the rapid movement of a luminous phenomenon.
description: On January 20, 2010, at approximately 10:30 PM, a person observed a light moving rapidly from their doorstep. No unusual noises were heard during the phenomenon's east-west movement. The information provided in the questionnaire was too brief to allow for an investigation. Despite repeated requests from GEIPAN (the French National Gendarmerie Intervention Group) urging the witness to report to the police in order to initiate a preliminary inquiry, no further information has been obtained to advance the investigation of this case, which does not appear to be unusual (a distant, flickering light?). The case is weak (only one witness and a brief questionnaire). Due to a lack of information and the impossibility of conducting a full investigation (particularly regarding air traffic control), this case is classified as Class C.

summary: Observations of a luminous phenomenon: astronomical observations of Sirius.
description: Two neighboring witnesses observed a multi-colored luminous phenomenon that intrigued them. The luminous phenomenon was present in the same area of the sky for several hours. The characteristics described by the witnesses correspond to those well-known for observing an astronomical phenomenon. The level of strangeness of the observation is low, and Sirius was indeed located in the observed area of the sky. This case is fully explained and classified as Class A, like the observation of the star Sirius.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon following the witness in a car: probable sighting of an aircraft.
description: During a journey on the A4 motorway towards Strasbourg, a witness observed for a few minutes a light resembling Venus that appeared to accompany the vehicle. The light maintained a constant altitude and apparent speed from Vendenheim to Strasbourg, where the witness lost sight of it as it was obscured by buildings. This case of observation is slightly unusual and most likely corresponds to a misidentification of the approach lights of a passenger aircraft, the aircraft being observed head-on. This case is class B: probable sighting of an aircraft.

summary: Atmospheric reentry of a bolide.
description: On January 13, 2010, at 6:35 PM, a motorist observed an intense luminous phenomenon lasting 6 to 7 seconds, which intrigued him. A fireball with a southwest-north trajectory crossed the sky very quickly before disappearing over the horizon. Another witness to this phenomenon later shared their account on a website. An atmospheric reentry of a bolide or meteor was recorded by the French Meteorological Network that day at 5:35 PM UTC, which corresponds to 6:35 PM French time. It was particularly visible in the Gironde region.

summary: Observation of three lights forming a triangle.
description: A witness reported an observation made by telephone on January 6, 2010, at 8:40 PM. For a few seconds, this driver and his passenger observed a stationary luminous phenomenon consisting of three light yellow lights forming a triangle, the size of which was compared to that of an airplane. Despite several follow-up attempts, the witness did not provide sufficient information for GEIPAN to conduct an investigation. This case is classified as Class C due to lack of information.

summary: Observations of the passage of an orange luminous phenomenon in the sky: probable observation of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On Wednesday, January 6, 2010, at approximately 7:30 PM, a motorist and his passengers observed an orange glow moving slowly across the sky. Of slight strangeness and inconsistency, this observation has all the characteristics of a misidentification as a Thai lantern, although its position and direction remain uncertain. This case is classified as Class B: probable sighting of a Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of the passage of a dark triangular mass delimited by yellow-orange lights at each end: unexplained phenomenon.
description: On January 4, 2010, at approximately 7:45 PM, a witness out for a walk was intrigued by the east-west movement of a large, dark, triangular shape with faint, yellow-orange luminous circles at each end. The speed was constant, and no unusual noise was heard during the 10 to 15 seconds of observation. No other eyewitness accounts were collected. The investigation confirmed and clarified the witness's testimony, lending credence to their statement. This strange sighting, unlike typical misinterpretations, was also inconsistent with the observation of a passing airliner, especially since the witness was very experienced in observing aircraft. The testimony would be consistent with a 2.5-meter-long model aircraft or drone flying at an altitude of 150 meters at approximately 35-150 km/h below the radar center of air traffic control (Charles de Gaulle Airport). It seems highly unlikely, however, that this type of craft would fly in an urban environment, at night, on a winter evening; this hypothesis, although potentially consistent with the observation, was not accepted due to a lack of other conclusive evidence. This strange sighting was reported by only one witness, without photos or videos; despite the quality of the testimony, this case remains of moderate consistency. GEIPAN classifies this strange and moderately consistent case in category D1, as an unexplained phenomenon.

summary: Probable sighting of Thai lanterns.
description: On January 3, 2010, a witness observed three round lights passing directly overhead from his garden. No sound was heard. They disappeared instantly. The described characteristics of the observation (three round lights at low altitude moving together and then 'disappearing' due to the fuel running out), as well as the strong suspicions raised by the initial findings of the police investigation, correspond to the probable observation of sky lanterns.

summary: Observations of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On January 1, 2010, at approximately 8:10 PM, numerous people witnessed a luminous phenomenon in the sky. Eight witness statements were received by the gendarmerie: two statements (T4 and T5 on the official police report) likely correspond to the observation of a lantern over the mainland (seen from Fouras and St. Augustin) but are not related to the object seen on the island by the other six witnesses. The person who launched the "lecher" (a type of lantern) in Saint-Pierre d'Oléron came forward voluntarily to the gendarmerie and declared that, between 8:00 PM and 8:15 PM on January 1, 2010, a "wishing balloon," traditionally used at parties and birthdays in the Netherlands, had released a "wishing balloon." This is a Class A case.

summary: Observation of the slow movement of a red ball in the sky: probable observation of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On the night of December 31, 2009, to January 1, 2010, at 12:30 a.m., a witness was intrigued by the slow movement of a red ball with a yellow outline across the sky. The phenomenon was observed for approximately three minutes before suddenly "leaving." Slightly strange and very inconsistent, this observation is likely a case of mistaken identity with a Thai lantern. This case is classified as Class B: probable observation of a Thai lantern.
